title: The tenants left the radio on

blocks.text: In April 1932, Nick Hannegraf spotted two of his mother’s tenants in True Detective Mysteries. The men renting at 1031 South Robert Street in West St. Paul were Alvin Karpis and Fred Barker. The state investigators’ report says Hannegraf had also taken down license plate numbers from cars coming and going.

Hannegraf said the departing tenants left the door open, the gas on, the radio playing, and part of a cooked meal on the table. The FBI’s later summary adds that his mother had seen the tenants carrying a violin case. Its contents are unknown, and the two reports differ on the sequence of the departure.

sourceLink.label: Read the 1932 investigators’ report

title: The café that got padlocked over ginger ale

blocks.text: Frank Cloutier and the Victoria Café Orchestra recorded “Moonshiner’s Dance” at the Lowry Hotel in 1927. The record preserves the sound of the band that played at the Frogtown café. Historian Kurt Gegenhuber describes the party favors handed out there, including little tin saxophones the customers could toot.

Gegenhuber traces a six-month closure order to March 1928, after Prohibition agents reported that waiters served ginger ale and ice to patrons who brought their own liquor. In a separate raid that December, former assistant Ramsey County attorney Allan McGill punched a federal agent. He later said he thought the café was being held up.

sourceLink.label: Hear “Moonshiner’s Dance” at Smithsonian Folkways

title: The Green Lantern and the pork chop sandwich

blocks.text: John Quinn shot and killed Frank Ventress behind the Green Lantern café on Wabasha Street in March 1931. Quinn claimed self-defense. A jury convicted him of second-degree murder, and the Minnesota Supreme Court upheld the conviction.

In 2019, the Pioneer Press followed researcher Jeff Neuberger as he tried to place some old police photographs. He and historian Jim Sazevich used the ornament atop a synagogue pillar to identify a building in one view. Three booths and a menu board advertising spaghetti and a pork chop sandwich matched witness descriptions. Several photos carry the same case mark. One exterior view with that mark is dated May 1930, before the shooting. Whether these photos were used at Quinn’s trial remains unresolved.

sourceLink.label: Read the Minnesota Supreme Court opinion

title: Edna Murray’s three escapes

blocks.text: Edna Murray was convicted in a Kansas City robbery in 1925. The FBI later recorded that she escaped from Missouri State Penitentiary three times. In December 1932, Murray and Irene McCann got out by sawing through their cell bars. A 1925 newspaper called Murray the “Kiss-Me” bandit. The alleged kiss behind the nickname remains unverified.

Murray went to trial in Saint Paul’s Federal Courts Building in April 1935 in proceedings arising from the Bremer kidnapping. The charges against her were dismissed in May. She went back to Missouri to serve time for the earlier robbery and the escape.

sourceLink.label: Read the FBI case summary

title: The print on the gasoline can

blocks.text: According to the FBI’s investigation summary, Arthur “Doc” Barker, Volney Davis, and Harry Campbell had surgery near Toledo to alter their faces and fingerprints. The report says their fingers hurt so badly afterward that companions, including Edna Murray, had to feed them.

A discarded gasoline can bore a print attributed to Barker. The Minnesota Historical Society’s account says a Wisconsin farmer found it. The FBI summary records that the can came into evidence over a defense objection at the Bremer trial in Saint Paul.

sourceLink.label: Read the FBI case summary

title: The Cleveland notebook

blocks.text: On August 30, 1933, robbers took the Swift and Company payroll outside the post office in the neighboring city of South St. Paul. Officer Leo Pavlak was killed and another officer was wounded.

A later raid in Cleveland turned up a notebook containing a route. Federal investigators traced its starting point to Stockyards National Bank. A 1936 FBI memo says agents followed the route and concluded that it was the getaway route from the payroll robbery.

sourceLink.label: Read the FBI memo on the route

title: Dinner at the Hollyhocks Inn

blocks.text: When federal agents interviewed Hollyhocks Inn proprietor Jack Peifer in October 1934, he told them he knew Frank Nash was an escaped federal prisoner. Peifer recalled that Nash and his wife had eaten at his Saint Paul inn and talked about heading north to visit her relatives. He put the dinner about ten days before Nash died in the Kansas City Massacre.

Peifer denied knowing anything about the killing. In a separate Saint Paul case, a jury convicted him in the kidnapping of brewer William Hamm. The Associated Press reported that Peifer received a 30-year sentence on July 31, 1936, and died that day.

sourceLink.label: Read the FBI interview file

title: The FBI’s improvised handcuffs

blocks.text: Federal agents arrested Alvin Karpis in New Orleans on May 1, 1936. The FBI’s later account describes a problem that came up as agents closed in on his car. They had arrived without handcuffs, so one agent took off his necktie and used it to bind Karpis’s hands.
An Associated Press dispatch reported that agents flew Karpis back to Saint Paul in chains. He later pleaded guilty in the William Hamm kidnapping and received a life sentence.

sourceLink.label: Read the FBI’s account of the arrest

title: The election bet with a death clause

blocks.text: On April 9, 1908, someone wrote out the terms of a bet on a sheet of Merchants Hotel stationery. Richard T. O’Connor backed David W. Faulder for mayor with $1,000. Republican industrialist Philip W. Herzog bet $600 on Joseph McKibbin. If either bettor or either candidate died before the election, the wager was void.

Richard was the police chief’s younger brother and a Democratic party boss. Herzog signed the receipt and addressed it to Pierce Butler, a railroad lawyer who later joined the U.S. Supreme Court. The surviving paper records the terms of the wager. Whether either man collected is unknown.

sourceLink.label: See the wager receipt on page 23

title: What the dig found at Nina Clifford’s

blocks.text: In 1997, work on the new Science Museum site exposed the foundations of Nina Clifford’s brothel at 147 South Washington Street. Archaeologists compared what they found near the front steps with what they found in the backyard. Tableware and food remains gave them clues about what customers and residents ate and used. The researchers also found evidence of poor health among the people who lived there.
A local story held that a secret tunnel connected the brothel to the Minnesota Club. The Minnesota Historical Society reports that the team found no tunnel in the area it excavated.

sourceLink.label: Read about the Washington Street excavation

title: The florist’s extra faucet

blocks.text: Helen Warren Pfleger started at the Saint Paul Prohibition Office in 1925. When agents went out on an investigation, she sometimes stayed late at the switchboard so the office could keep in touch. She also remembered agents trading their usual clothes for worn outfits to avoid being recognized.

Pfleger’s 1975 memoir recounts a search at a flower shop. An agent was about to leave when he spotted an extra faucet behind a stand of ferns. In her telling, liquor flowed when he turned it. Pfleger tells the story secondhand and leaves the shop unnamed.

sourceLink.label: Read Pfleger’s memoir

title: Scotch labels and body rub

blocks.text: In June 1925, federal agents said they broke through steel and barred doors at a Wheeler Avenue bungalow. Behind them, they reported finding an operation that turned body rub into liquor bottled to look like Scotch. The St. Paul Daily News printed a picture of the house and doors. The haul reportedly included capping equipment and cases labeled White Horse, Old Parr, and Haig and Haig.

Historian Paul R. Gold says Prohibition agents destroyed all but one bottle before Sam Taran’s trial that October. Taran’s lawyer argued that a landlord might know nothing about what went on inside his property. The jury acquitted Taran.

sourceLink.label: Read the raid account in Ramsey County History

title: The dummy ransom package

blocks.text: Two armed men seized 20-year-old Haskell Bohn near his family’s Summit Avenue home on June 30, 1932. According to the Associated Press, they handed his chauffeur a note demanding $35,000. The demand was written in pencil on cheap paper.

After Bohn returned, police told the AP they had used a dummy package of money to catch three local men who allegedly tried to get $10,000 by promising to bring him home. The men’s case outcomes remain unclear. Bohn’s father said he paid no ransom. A later indictment alleged a payment in the kidnapping case itself.

sourceLink.label: Read the 1932 report of the dummy package

title: The fingerprint file and the $100 fine

blocks.text: At his 1936 federal trial in Saint Paul, Harry Sawyer testified that he had never been convicted of a felony. The prosecutor asked investigators to check. Agent S. W. Hardy found a 1918 Minneapolis arrest filed under Harry Stanley. A clerk said he could produce the fingerprint card and photograph plate under police file No. 16479. A detective recalled firing a warning shot during the arrest.

The court entries used another name, Harry Sandelvoich. They recorded a guilty plea for tampering with an automobile and a $100 fine that he paid. The prosecutor told Hardy that he could not use the conviction to challenge Sawyer’s testimony because it was a misdemeanor.

sourceLink.label: Read Agent Hardy’s report on Sawyer’s old arrest

title: The keys Eddie Green was carrying

blocks.text: A federal memo says that after the Lincoln Court shootout, agents tracked baggage from an apartment on Marshall Avenue to a second Saint Paul location. They waited for Eddie Green to collect it. Agents shot Green on April 3, 1934. He died in the hospital a week later.

The memo says agents found keys on Green and that he told them the keys belonged to Dillinger. It also says a gunstock found at the Marshall Avenue apartment appeared to fit a machine gun left behind at Lincoln Court.

sourceLink.label: Read the April 10 memo on Eddie Green

title: The airline uniforms and the Bremer kidnapping

blocks.text: On January 13, 1934, three Northwest Airways employees in uniform were near Portland Avenue and St. Alban Street in Saint Paul. Federal investigators later concluded that two gang members leaving a meeting mistook the men for police officers following them. The investigators said the gang members opened fire, badly wounding one of the workers, and that Harry Sawyer then pressed to put off the Bremer kidnapping.

Radio operator Roy McCord survived. The following year, federal agents asked him whether he recognized Arthur “Doc” Barker as the shooter. McCord told them he could not identify Barker as the man who fired.

sourceLink.label: Read the federal reconstruction, p. 17

title: The Gleeman brothers’ railroad car

blocks.text: Burton Stevens was shot and killed at the entrance to the Dreis drugstore at Ninth and St. Peter streets in Saint Paul on February 16, 1925. Abe and Ben Gleeman were convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison. They gave the court a different account when they asked for a new trial.

The brothers’ new account described a Twin Cities liquor syndicate and a recent dispute over a railroad car full of alcohol. Ben also said he brought a truckload of liquor to an Eighth Street garage on the morning of the shooting. He blamed another man for Stevens’s death. The Minnesota Supreme Court upheld the denial of a new trial.

sourceLink.label: Read the Gleeman brothers’ appeal

title: What a car buyer heard by his furnace

blocks.text: Mark Wynn ran an auto dealership on University Avenue. A customer named Cooke testified that Wynn came to his house in February 1927 with another man. When Cooke went down to his furnace, Wynn followed and said the man upstairs was there to keep him from running away.

Wynn said Sam Taran and armed associates held him for ten days and made him forge car contracts. A Minneapolis finance company paid $700 for the note and mortgage on a purported sale. The Minnesota Supreme Court found independent evidence that Taran received the money and upheld his grand larceny conviction in 1929.

sourceLink.label: Read the Minnesota Supreme Court opinion

title: The burglary that left the diamonds

blocks.text: Alice McQuillan Dunn was killed at her family’s Selby Avenue home in April 1917. Her diamond rings and watch were left behind. According to testimony summarized on appeal, the men who broke in had been hired to kill her and were supposed to make it look like a burglary. In their account, high water forced two of them to change their route after they left in a taxi.

The court looked for other evidence to test the accomplices’ account. Frank Dunn acknowledged visiting the drugstore where one man said he and Alice had been pointed out. Dunn also visited a safe-deposit vault on the day of the murder. A jury found him guilty of first-degree murder, and the Minnesota Supreme Court upheld the denial of a new trial.

sourceLink.label: Read the Minnesota Supreme Court opinion

title: The gun Herbert Scott remembered seeing twice

blocks.text: In a 1979 interview, former Saint Paul patrolman Herbert Scott recalled an encounter on Robert Street with his partner, Boyd Carrier. Scott said they took a .45 automatic from Tommy Carroll and brought him to headquarters. The detectives, he said, told the two patrolmen to leave Carroll there and said they would write the report.

Scott said that about two hours later he saw Carroll back on Robert Street. Carroll opened his coat, and Scott believed he was looking at the same gun. Scott said Carrier had written and turned in a report anyway. When the patrolmen went looking for it later, Scott recalled, they could not find it.

sourceLink.label: Read Herbert Scott’s interview, pages 17–18

title: What Bernice Fisher remembered from her porch

blocks.text: Homer Van Meter, a Dillinger associate, was killed in Saint Paul on August 23, 1934. Bernice Fisher grew up at 193 West University Avenue. In a memoir written decades later, she remembered standing on her front porch and watching police jump out of their squad cars and run up the alley across the street.

Patrolman Herbert Scott remembered answering a call on University Avenue about a dog struck by a car. He heard a volley farther east and could not tell at first whether it was gunfire or firecrackers. He went to look and, in his 1979 account, found Van Meter in the alley behind a filling station near Marion Street.

sourceLink.label: Read Bernice Fisher’s memoir, page 25

title: The bartender’s ring and Roosevelt’s veto

blocks.text: A revenue inspector reporting a liquor sale in 1919 described a bartender with a yellow-stone pinky ring and a pointed little fingernail. He had heard the surname Rogowski. The original allegation, as recorded in a congressional letter, came to eight glasses at 25 cents each. John Rogowski of South St. Paul pleaded guilty and paid a $100 fine. John and his brother Alex paid another $1,281.25 in taxes and penalties under protest.

In seeking repayment, the brothers pointed to another Rogowski associated with a saloon on South Wabasha Street in Saint Paul. A Senate committee recommended reimbursement. In 1938, President Franklin D. Roosevelt vetoed the bill, citing the earlier rejection of their refund claim and the expiration of the deadline for filing suit.

sourceLink.label: Read the Senate report and the inspector’s description

title: The jury heard the needle skip

blocks.text: The jurors at Fred W. Raasch’s trial listened to recorded phone calls through headsets. The calls came from Cedar 5328, a line that bypassed the Saint Paul police switchboard. Operators tapped the line and recorded calls with a device the court called a pamograph. When the playback needle skipped a groove, the court replayed the recording so the jury could hear the missing words.

The typed transcripts helped witnesses and the court follow the calls. The recordings went into evidence, while the transcripts stayed out. Raasch was convicted of malfeasance for helping gamblers evade the law. The Minnesota Supreme Court upheld the denial of a new trial.

sourceLink.label: Read the Minnesota Supreme Court opinion

title: Hamm and Bolton on the same flight

blocks.text: On July 23, 1933, five weeks after William Hamm Jr. was kidnapped, Bryan Bolton boarded a Northwest Airways flight from Saint Paul toward Chicago. Bolton later told federal agents he saw Hamm and an agent on the plane. Bolton got off in Madison. The FBI said the agent’s statement and the airline’s passenger manifests backed up Bolton’s account.

The FBI later named Bolton as one of the men involved in Hamm’s abduction. In July 1936, the Associated Press reported that Bolton had pleaded guilty in the case and that the prosecutor expected him to be the government’s principal witness.

sourceLink.label: Read the FBI memo on the Northwest Airways flight

title: The car key and the moonshine room

blocks.text: Prohibition agents testified that they bought moonshine at what looked like a grocery, candy, and cigar store on East Thirteenth Street. On a later visit, Weinberg handed over two Yale keys he said were for his car. An agent tried one in a locked door off the courtyard. It opened.

Agents reported finding moonshine in five-gallon jugs, bottles under a couch, and two funnels on the wall above it. The defendants disputed the testimony. A jury found them guilty on possession and sale counts, and the federal judge denied their application for a writ of error.

sourceLink.label: Read the federal opinion on the keys and the search

title: The Shell signs and five flashes

blocks.text: On February 6, 1934, Walter Magee took Edward Bremer’s ransom to 969 University Avenue in Saint Paul. According to the FBI’s account, Magee moved the money into a waiting Chevrolet coupe with Shell signs on both doors. He found the keys and another set of instructions in a pocket in the driver’s door.

The note sent Magee to Farmington to follow a bus bound for Rochester. Four red lights marked where he was to turn. On a gravel road, a car behind him flashed its headlights five times and he left two boxes by the road. Agents later showed an original Shell sign to a sign writer and contacted the sign painters’ union.

sourceLink.label: Read the FBI’s inquiry about the Shell sign

title: Wallpaper and strawberry shortcake

blocks.text: After his release, Edward Bremer told investigators what he remembered of the room where his captors held him. The FBI said he described the wallpaper in enough detail for agents to find a similar pattern sold by a large mail-order house. They showed him a sample, which he recognized as similar to the paper he had seen.

Bremer remembered dogs barking and children playing close to the house. He recalled feeling where enamel had chipped off the toilet lever. The FBI summary also records something he remembered being served in the middle of winter: fresh strawberry shortcake.

sourceLink.label: Read the FBI summary of Bremer’s observations

title: The Squeezor beer bottle

blocks.text: In June 1933, Saint Paul police recovered a beer bottle at 804 Vernon Avenue. A federal investigator’s letter quotes the telegram that came back after police submitted the print. The identification bureau had matched it to Frank Nash’s right thumb. When Nash handled the bottle remains unknown.

The bottle was one of six labeled Squeezor. Agents showed photographs to neighborhood shopkeepers. They found two nearby businesses that carried the brand, a drugstore and the St. Clair Street Shop. Neither led them to the sale. The report says Saint Paul police were keeping the bottle.

sourceLink.label: Read the shopkeeper interviews, page 14

title: Grand Avenue and the fire hose

blocks.text: After a Minneapolis bank robbery that killed three people in December 1932, authorities traced some of the money to Larry De Vol’s Grand Avenue apartment in Saint Paul. A news report called him Lawrence Barton. The FBI’s case summary says De Vol pleaded guilty to murder and received a life sentence at Stillwater.

In June 1936, De Vol escaped from the state hospital at St. Peter. The Medford Mail Tribune reported that people in the group struck guards with chair legs, used tools to pry loose a barred window and took a fire hose to climb down.

sourceLink.label: Read the 1936 newspaper account of the escape

title: Out of Ancker Hospital in slippers

blocks.text: A newspaper clipping reports that two men attacked and wounded former boxer Sam Taran at his Saint Paul apartment. Historian Paul R. Gold dates the attack to Christmas Eve 1925. Gold says the wounded Taran threw one of the men, Billy Alexander, down a staircase. Alexander was taken to Ancker Hospital.

Gold reports that Alexander left the hospital around midnight on January 21, 1926. The temperature was below zero, and he was wearing slippers, pajamas, and a robe. Police suspected friends had a car waiting.

sourceLink.label: Read the attack and escape account, page 16

title: Tierney asked to hear the record

blocks.text: A March letter in the Bremer files describes federal agent John E. Brennan asking Saint Paul assistant police inspector Charles Tierney about a purported recording. The claim was that Tierney had told someone to say nothing to Brennan. Tierney denied the conversation.

Tierney told Brennan they should go to Daily News editor Howard Kahn and ask him to play the record or retract the claim. Brennan declined. Stein also reported that Tierney pledged to cooperate with the Bureau.

sourceLink.label: Read the letter about Tierney’s interview

title: The former police chief’s gold

blocks.text: At a civil service hearing, former Saint Paul police chief Thomas A. Brown said he had exchanged $900 in gold for currency under a federal gold order, according to the Saint Paul Daily News. Its September 1936 editorial also said he had changed a $1,000 bill at a bank, made loans, and used three safe-deposit boxes.

The paper said Brown’s monthly police salary had never topped $158 except during his two years as chief. It asked how the figures fit together and acknowledged there could be an explanation. The source of the money remains unresolved.

sourceLink.label: Read the Daily News editorial on Brown’s hearing

title: Slots on rubber pads and beer on ice

blocks.text: Saint Paul police knocked at an East Eleventh Street apartment in March 1936 and asked for a man they knew as Slim. On the way through the kitchen they found about ten cases of beer, some on ice, and about two dozen whiskey and highball glasses. In the front room sat two slot machines with money inside, both on rubber pads.

Kaasa said some of the liquor and other items belonged to a man who was in Winnipeg. He said he did not know how the machines got there. The officers had no search warrant, and the court heard no proof of an actual sale. The Minnesota Supreme Court upheld his conviction for keeping liquor for sale without a city license.

sourceLink.label: Read the Minnesota Supreme Court opinion

title: Mystic Caverns advertised two thousand mirrors

blocks.text: In 1933, ads for Mystic Caverns sent drivers down the river road under the High Bridge to a neon skull and crossbones. The club promised a spectacle with two thousand mirrors and music by Jack Foster’s Ten Cavemen. Historian Greg Brick reproduces one of the ads in his account of Saint Paul’s caves.

Brick says Foster co-owned Mystic Caverns and led the Saint Paul police band. The Minnesota Historical Society’s finding aid for Paul Maccabee’s research lists Robert “Frisco Dutch” Steinhardt as a casino operator there. Brick traces the club’s 1934 closure to a grand jury gambling investigation. Castle Royal was a separate cave nightclub.

sourceLink.label: See the Mystic Caverns advertisement, page 113

title: Dillinger’s Hudson and the black wire wheels

blocks.text: Irving Gleeman brought a 1932 Chevrolet to Potthoff Motor Company on Bates Avenue in Saint Paul. Dealer W. J. Potthoff told investigators he offered $331 toward a new Hudson, the amount set by the trade code, and that Gleeman ultimately accepted it. Potthoff also said Gleeman insisted on black wire wheels and agreed to take the car first and change the wheels later.

Gleeman remembered the same $331 offer. He said he held out for $375 and went ahead when Tom Filben approved. Filben supplied a name for the order, and Gleeman said he told the dealer to put down any address. One passage gives the name as Carl T. Hellman, the alias Dillinger used at Lincoln Court.

An April 2 interview with Potthoff gives $375 as the trade-in allowance on the March 29 transfer agreement. That matches Gleeman’s figure. Gleeman said the dealer credited his $206 check as $250 to account for the $44 above the code price. The federal report also identifies this Hudson as the car in Dillinger’s possession when he escaped from Lincoln Court.

sourceLink.label: Read the dealer and Gleeman interviews in the federal file

title: The price of police protection

blocks.text: Ida Dorsey opened a brothel at 151 South Washington Street in March 1913, in a building previously owned by Nina Clifford. At the 1914 graft trial, Dorsey said she had met with police chief Martin Flanagan about opening for business. In historian Penny Petersen’s account of the testimony, Dorsey said she offered references from Minneapolis officials.

According to Petersen’s account of the trial, Clifford testified that Dorsey paid her $4,000. Clifford said $1,000 went toward the house and the remaining $3,000 was to go to officials and underworld figures to secure protection for the business. Within months of its opening, the chief ordered the city’s brothels closed and Dorsey’s operation shut down.

A February 20, 1914, dispatch from Saint Paul reported that a jury had convicted former chief Martin J. Flanagan and former chief of detectives Fred Turner of bribery. Both had been sentenced to state prison for terms of up to a year. The dispatch describes the charge as accepting $300 in exchange for protection and leaves the payer unnamed.

sourceLink.label: Read the 1914 dispatch on the verdict

title: The shirt with no label

blocks.text: Edward Bremer’s kidnappers gave him a shirt, socks and a union suit when they let him go. The Saint Paul office sent the clothes to a federal lab. Examiner C. A. Appel found the shirt label missing, but the old stitch holes were still there. The collar button measured 0.3989 inches across. A number in blue crayon remained inside the shirt. On the socks, he pointed to the way the heel stitches gathered.

The Saint Paul agents cross-checked towns where two or more of the articles appeared to be sold. Their February 27 report named Mueller Clothing Company in Windom and J. H. Conley in Watertown. Both looked like places to ask about the shirt and underwear. The working list gave agents shops to visit. It had no receipt tying either store to the kidnappers.

On March 5, agent W. C. Ryan interviewed Gustave Mueller. Mueller said he stocked a lighter shirt in a different style, had been sent a different brand when he ordered the underwear, and didn’t carry the socks. The Windom stop that looked promising in the index narrowed the search instead.

sourceLink.label: Read the lab report on the clothes

title: A new lease, the same bar

blocks.text: The first floor at 905 West Seventh Street was used as a soft drink bar. Prohibition agents described a bar, back bar, mirror and glassware like the fittings of a saloon. In court, the parties agreed that four alcohol sales took place there on April 6, 1925, and that liquor was found nine days later.

Owner Peter Engler evicted Leonard Ayd after the April violations. On May 1, John Ryshavy took over under a new lease. He ran a soft drink and food business, and the parties agreed he had never been charged with a violation. The appeals court noted that the business carried on with the same equipment.

The appeals court ruled that changing tenants was insufficient to show the unlawful use had ended. It upheld an order keeping the premises closed for one year from April 11, 1927. The case was a civil action about the use of the property.

sourceLink.label: Read the federal appeals court opinion

title: Four mail pouches and a Plymouth key

blocks.text: A Post Office Department circular says armed robbers held up a mail train at the Erie station in Garrettsville, Ohio, on November 7, 1935. Two men entered the mail car. The circular lists what they carried off: two pouches of registered mail and two pouches of ordinary mail.

A postal inspector gave the FBI a description of the getaway car: a gunmetal gray 1935 Plymouth with two windshield wipers, two taillights and a trunk. His description went down to the key number, MP 802. At that point the inspectors suspected Alvin Karpis and Harry Campbell, two men already wanted in the Saint Paul Bremer case.

The FBI’s 1936 case summary says the later investigation identified Karpis and Campbell as participants in the mail robbery. Its account of the Ohio holdup sits in the investigation of Edward Bremer’s kidnapping in Saint Paul. The records here establish what investigators concluded. They leave the outcome of any charges over the train robbery unresolved.

sourceLink.label: Read the postal circular and the Plymouth description

title: Seven glasses after closing

blocks.text: On Sunday, February 21, two officers noticed parked cars outside the licensed beer parlor at 419 West Wheelock Parkway. The curtains were drawn and the doors locked. They knocked at 3:15 a.m. and waited a few minutes before someone let them in. The city’s Sunday closing hours ran from 2 to 5 a.m.

The officers reported finding a man at the bar with a partly filled glass. A man and a woman sat in a booth with seven partly filled beer glasses in front of them. Four men in work clothes were hiding in the basement. Other people were in the back of the building. This was an after-hours case at a licensed beer parlor; the opinion gives no gang connection.

The owners testified that they stopped the music at closing and invited a few people to stay to plan a surprise for the following week. They said no beer was sold during the discussion. The Minnesota Supreme Court concluded that the officers’ testimony supported the inference that the parlor was still open for business. It affirmed the convictions.

sourceLink.label: Read the court’s account of the beer parlor

title: The telegram under the carpet

blocks.text: After Dillinger fled Lincoln Court, federal agents inventoried what was left in the apartment. Alongside the papers were photographs. One showed a boy in a cherry tree. A pencil note on the back named him as John Dillinger and put him at about ten or eleven. The inventory also records a picture of a small boy in a wagon and one of Dillinger in naval uniform.

The inventory also led agents to a road chart. The Kansas City office reported that agent O. C. Dewey traced the route from Newton National Bank in Iowa to Saint Paul. Investigators suspected it showed a getaway route and sent the chart to the federal laboratory.

After the agents took away the inventoried items, building manager Daisy Coffey told them she had found part of a Western Union telegram under the carpet. The agents transcribed what remained. The report leaves the sender, recipient and meaning of “three” open.

sourceLink.label: Read the Lincoln Court inventory and the telegram transcription

title: Gleckman and the jury’s doctor bill

blocks.text: After Leon Gleckman’s federal tax conviction, the clerk entered $6,193.30 in prosecution costs against him. The bill included meals and lodging for jurors and payments to a doctor who had treated several of them during the trials. Gleckman objected and appealed. The disputed expenses of providing the judge and jury came to about $2,500.

The bill also listed fees and mileage for federal investigator Michael F. Malone. He had been needed at the trial, the court said, but an agreement between the lawyers made his testimony unnecessary. The appeals judges said the bill could include his necessary travel and subsistence under the rule for federal employees. The original fees and mileage had to be recalculated on that basis.

The appeals court upheld the tax convictions. It reached a separate decision on the bill. The cost of providing a judge and jury was a government expense, so the disputed tribunal charges had to come off. The court directed the lower court to recalculate the costs.

sourceLink.label: Read the appeals court’s ruling on the bill

title: The whistle kept going

blocks.text: Edward Bremer remembered a factory whistle and a siren from the place where the Barker–Karpis gang held him. According to a June 1934 report from the Saint Paul office, the morning whistle was already sounding when the siren swelled. The siren fell away and the whistle carried on a little longer. Bremer went out with agents to compare sounds for himself. A Madison streetcar bell resembled one he remembered hearing on the way to the hideout, but none of the towns they visited matched the timing he gave.

Saint Paul sent letters asking about local sounds and ranked towns by how many reported sounds might fit. The replies took an unexpected turn. According to the bureau, some ministers thought agents objected to their bells, and some civic officials asked whether a new federal law restricted sirens. The Rev. Oscar Rockoff of Brookfield, Illinois, checked his church records for investigators. His bell had tolled 48 times on one occasion, marking a parishioner’s death and age.

By April 1935 the bureau had found the hideout. Saint Paul’s D. M. Ladd wrote to Washington asking permission to destroy the circular letters. He told the director he saw no future use for them. J. Edgar Hoover approved the request on May 7. The exchange records the decision. What happened to every letter remains unclear.

sourceLink.label: Read the Saint Paul office’s account of the sound search

title: The gold basketball at Wildwood

blocks.text: On the night of August 13, 1930, state investigators came upon a parked car near Wildwood Amusement Park. A United Press report says its headlights caught their attention. Three men died in the shooting. The report says the investigators had been in the area looking into a tip about George “Bugs” Moran.

On page two, the report turns to a small object. A gold basketball hung from a chain on the man the paper named as Frank Coleman of Kansas City. The inscription read “K. C. ’20.” The paper said police used the token along with other items in identifying him.

The Associated Press named Coleman and Sammy Stein. It said police believed the third man was a Saint Paul underworld figure called “Butch” Myers, whose name was spelled differently across the wire reports. Police suspected a quarrel over slot machine concessions. The names and the proposed motive were still being reported as investigators worked.

sourceLink.label: Read the dispatch and turn to page two for the basketball

title: The dishes they left on Grand Avenue

blocks.text: Coming home from a basketball game in early March 1933, the Parnells saw cars and people moving between two Grand Avenue apartment buildings. In the account he gave federal investigators, building custodian Mr. Parnell called the police and slipped into the laundry room to watch. A door squeaked. He said a man in the hall spun around with a revolver, and that he kept still until the man went on.

The Parnells recalled that police took away clothing and bedding and left the dishes and silverware behind. On April 26 a mover came for those with a penciled note addressed to a man named Hardwick. Agents later sent the note and a separate letter for handwriting comparison. The Parnells said photos of several gang figures resembled people they had seen, and left the occupants’ identities unresolved.

Agents working the Edward Bremer case looked up the utility deposits for the Grand Avenue apartments. The file records one six-dollar deposit for gas and electric service and two similar deposits. Two refund checks came back unclaimed. The third did not come back, and the utility showed no credit remaining on that account. The agent kept tracings of signatures from the service applications.

sourceLink.label: Read the Grand Avenue interviews and the mover’s note in the case file

title: The Babe Ruth picture in Sankey’s file

blocks.text: Haskell Bohn took the stand in Saint Paul at Fern Sankey’s trial in June 1933. The Associated Press reported that he named Verne Sankey and Ray Robinson as the two men who abducted him from the rear of his home the previous summer. The paper said Robinson had pleaded guilty. Verne Sankey was still being sought.

In January 1934, Ramsey County Attorney M. F. Kinkead told the Associated Press that a search at Sankey’s South Dakota ranch turned up a file about the earnings of boxer Jack Dempsey and baseball star Babe Ruth. He described a picture of Ruth on one sheet with a short notation below it. From the papers, Kinkead inferred that Sankey might have intended to kidnap the two athletes.

Federal agents arrested Sankey in a Chicago barber shop on January 31. Federal investigator Melvin Purvis told the Associated Press that Sankey admitted taking part in Bohn’s kidnapping and a separate kidnapping in Denver. The same report repeats Kinkead’s accusation about the athletes. The papers place the accusation and the reported confession side by side.

sourceLink.label: Read the dispatch describing the Ruth and Dempsey file

title: Ben Franklin at the Frederic

blocks.text: While Arthur “Doc” Barker awaited trial in Saint Paul, he asked special deputy Jack Hession to carry notes between his cell block and Mildred Kuhlman. A June 16 letter from the federal office says Sheriff Thomas Gibbons arranged for agents to get copies of the notes Hession carried before he delivered them.

Hession said Barker suggested taking a room at the Frederic Hotel, where Kuhlman was staying, so he could reach her quickly. Hession said he registered as Ben Franklin and saw her nearly every day during his stay. In the account he gave agents, she did not know who he really was.

Hession submitted a bill for $26.50, including $21.50 for the room and the balance for telephone expenses. He said he had expected Barker to cover the costs, but Barker had been moved to Leavenworth. The Saint Paul office asked Washington whether it could pay the bill as a confidential expense.

sourceLink.label: Read the Saint Paul office’s letter about the notes and the bill

title: The judges went downstairs

blocks.text: A Milwaukee mail train reached Saint Paul at 2:45 p.m. with a special car attached. According to the Associated Press, Eddie McFadden and Gus Schaefer came off first, handcuffed together. Roger Touhy was cuffed to Willie Sharkey. Armed officers escorted the four men to jail to await proceedings in the William Hamm kidnapping case.

For a September hearing, federal judges J. W. Molyneaux and M. M. Joyce came to the Ramsey County jail. The Associated Press reported that the defendants were brought down from their upstairs cells to a basement courtroom guarded with machine guns. Holding the hearing inside the jail spared a street transfer. The judges denied separate trials and kept bail at $100,000 apiece.

When the trial opened in November, the Associated Press described deputy sheriffs with tear gas guns inside the courtroom and guards checking passes in the eighth-floor corridor. On November 28, a jury acquitted all four men of transporting Hamm across state lines and conspiring to do so.

title: The typewriter on the supply shelf

blocks.text: In the search for the machine that typed the Bremer ransom notes, a February 26 memo describes what the laboratory expected to find. A promising machine was to type three lines on paper like the kidnappers’ paper. One was the familiar sentence about the quick brown fox. The lab was looking for a 1929 portable Corona with pica type.

At L. C. Smith & Corona, the repair slips were filed by customer name. An agent reported looking through about five hundred slips and finding two for the type of machine in question. One described a Corona from a Saint Paul boiler and machinery company with a $1.50 repair bill. A separate memo describes the other machine, which had once used a slightly smudgy purple ribbon. The agent did not think that second machine was the one they sought.

A typewriter recovered from a Cleveland apartment occupied by Alvin Karpis and others went to Washington. A clerk found it on a supply-room shelf, in a case with a painted room number. An October letter says the shipment lacked the labels that would have routed it to the laboratory. By the time it reached the lab, staff reported that they could not obtain samples. It was an Underwood, and investigators were looking for a Corona in the Hamm and Bremer cases.

sourceLink.label: Read the supply-room memo and the October follow-up

title: The headline that buried Abe Wagner early

blocks.text: The Manchester Evening Herald ran a short Associated Press dispatch under the headline ‘Abie Wagner Slain.’ It relayed a claim by the New York Sun that the missing bootlegger had been killed two months earlier and sunk in the East River in a barrel of cement. The headline had the certainty of a death notice. The dispatch itself named another newspaper as its source.

Abe Wagner had gone west. Historian Anne E. Cowie describes the New York bootlegger posing as a fruit peddler in Saint Paul. On July 25 he was shot near Snelling and University avenues, twelve days after the dispatch put him in the East River.

Cowie writes that two men were convicted and given life sentences. A July 1933 bureau letter gives a different pair of names and dates the Saint Paul arrests to July 26, 1932. The sources agree on the victim. The bureau calls him Abe Wagner and describes him as a New York City gangster.

sourceLink.label: Read the 1932 report that put Wagner in the East River

title: The dress shop and the Silver Slipper

blocks.text: The Associated Press called him Moritz Rutman, a 27-year-old proprietor of a women’s dress shop. It reported that he had been held at a cottage near White Bear Lake for three days. Released early on October 8, he made his way home and was taken to a hospital.

Writing about the Ramsey County Attorney’s Office in 2000, Anne E. Cowie called him Morris Rutman and identified him as a bootlegger. Her account names Jack Ferrick and associates as the men who took Rutman from his Saint Paul home and held him at the Silver Slipper, a gambling spot in Mahtomedi.

Rutman said his captors demanded $50,000. A longer version of the dispatch reported that the police chief denied any payment and that friends had heard relatives paid. The amount paid, if any, remains unresolved in the dispatches.

sourceLink.label: Read the October 8 dispatch

title: The man who said he sold soap

blocks.text: When officers came to Lincoln Court on March 31, a man appeared in the hallway near Dillinger’s apartment. The Bureau’s later case history says he drew a gun when questioned and fled after shots were exchanged. The contemporary case file preserves the job he had claimed to do. He said he sold soap.

On April 8, an internal memo recorded how little the Saint Paul investigators could then prove. Agent Rufus Coulter thought Homer Van Meter might be the man. The memo notes a facial resemblance between Van Meter and Eddie Green in photographs, and says agents had found no Van Meter fingerprints in the apartments or on the guns they had examined.

Bessie Skinner told investigators that Van Meter came to the apartment she shared with Eddie Green later that day. She said he told her he had claimed to be a soap salesman and fired at the officer who questioned him. Her interview records what she said she heard afterward. The Bureau’s later history names Van Meter as the man in the hall.

sourceLink.label: Read the April 8 memo and Bessie Skinner’s interview in the file

title: The Buick spotted from a streetcar

blocks.text: In Paul R. Gold’s account, a man riding a Saint Paul streetcar looked out near University Avenue and Dale Street and spotted his missing Buick at a garage. It was a roadster valued at $1,400. The owner’s next clue was inside the car.

Gold says the owner took a closer look and found brochures from his own nut-shelling plant inside the roadster. He called police. Sam Taran, a boxer the papers called the Fighting Tailor who later became known for bootlegging, appeared before Judge Hugo Hanft on a car theft charge.

Gold writes that Taran was released after appearing in district court. The St. Paul Daily News account that Gold quotes calls him Sam Terrin and says Judge Hanft advised him to stick to the tailoring business. The account gives the advice and the release. Gold’s account gives no final disposition for the charge.

sourceLink.label: Read Gold’s account of the Buick and Judge Hanft

title: The hospital crowd and Hogan’s Christmas turkeys

blocks.text: After a bomb exploded in Danny Hogan’s car, the Associated Press reported that the Saint Paul bootlegger died that evening after surgery. In a later account, Star Tribune writer Curt Brown described bootleggers, gamblers, racketeers and a boxing champion turning up at the hospital to offer blood.

The Minneapolis Morning Tribune described the reputation Hogan had among some of the people who knew him. Then it made an unusual forecast, preserved in Curt Brown’s later article. ‘There will be some fewer turkey dinners in St. Paul this Christmas as a result of his death.’

In a later history of the St. Francis Hotel, Paul R. Gold wrote that more than 2,000 people attended Hogan’s funeral and that the flowers filled five cars. Gold recounts Harry Turgeon’s memory of looking around St. Mary’s Catholic Church and recognizing regulars from the hotel’s Granada Club.

sourceLink.label: Read the December 4 dispatch

title: A two-dollar delivery

blocks.text: A taxi driver brought two notes to the home of Hamm Brewing manager William Dunn. According to a June 17 United Press dispatch, police were already waiting there and arrested him. He said he had been paid two dollars to deliver the messages and had no idea what they said.

The June report said the driver thought a photo of Verne Sankey might show the man who handed him the messages. By the November trial, another man was in front of him. The caption entry for a 1933 press photograph names the driver as Leo J. Allison and says he thought Eddie McFadden resembled the man who gave him the note. The archive says he would not identify McFadden as the sender.

The Associated Press reported that the jury acquitted McFadden, Roger Touhy, Willie Sharkey and Gustav Schaefer on both federal charges. They faced counts of taking Hamm across state lines and conspiring to do so. The verdict resolved the charges against those four men. The verdict does not tell us who handed the driver the notes.

sourceLink.label: Read the first report of the $2 delivery

title: The coat left in 303

blocks.text: Patricia Cherrington later told federal agents that she, her sister and John Hamilton went to a Saint Paul restaurant after the shooting. They contacted Homer Van Meter, who she said took them to Harry Sawyer’s cottage near the city. They stayed for four days, she said, then hurried back to Saint Paul after a warning about a raid. The report gives no address for the cottage.

Bessie Skinner told agents what Van Meter told her after the shooting. In her account, the trio turned away a block from Lincoln Court and eventually went to McCormick’s restaurant. Someone drove them away in a Ford sedan. Skinner believed they went to Sawyer’s farm. Compare what she heard with what Cherrington said she did.

A federal witness outline for the Lincoln Court case says Werner Hanni was expected to describe what he found in Apartment 303. Amid the weapons and bulletproof vests, the outline listed a woman’s light tan coat with a platinum fox collar. It even named the store on the label. The owner’s name is missing from the entry.

sourceLink.label: Read the federal outline listing the coat

title: The goggles in the snow

blocks.text: At the end of his captivity, Edward Bremer was let out of a car in Rochester and told to count before uncovering his eyes. In one FBI account, he got to five and was told to start over because the car was still there. He waited until he heard it drive away, then pulled off the goggles and tossed them into the weeds.

Agent M. P. Glynn’s witness outline puts the search behind a red brick building, in the gap between the wall and a wire fence. Rochester detective George Rhode was with him. The goggles were in the weeds under about three inches of snow. Glynn sent them to the Bureau’s Saint Paul office.

The Bureau listed the welder’s goggles among the items it expected Bremer to identify. Its report said they were in Bureau custody and would go to the U.S. attorney in Saint Paul. The list gives their intended destination. It leaves open what happened to them after that.

sourceLink.label: Open Glynn’s recovery account in the FBI Vault

title: The ransom money under the hatband

blocks.text: In April 1934, an assistant cashier at Chicago’s Uptown State Bank remembered a customer who had come in about a week earlier to exchange small bills. According to Hoover’s memorandum, the cashier checked the serial numbers on some of the fives against the list from the Bremer kidnapping. He found matches. The Chicago office alerted other banks. Tellers at First National recognized the warning when William Vidler came in to exchange money on April 26, and agents took him into custody.

Agents followed the trail to Jack McLaughlin, son of the Chicago political figure known as Boss McLaughlin. A field report says Jack initially denied wearing a hat. At the rack he pointed to a gray felt hat, which sat about a size and a half too large when he tried it on. He next pointed to a brown flat-brimmed felt hat. Under its sweatband, agents reported finding two sealed envelopes of cash. Both the field report and Hoover’s memo linked some of that money to the Bremer ransom.

Vidler petitioned to recover $460 taken at his arrest. Saint Paul’s U.S. attorney said his office made no claim to hold that sum as evidence because it could not be identified as ransom money. If the money was to go back, Melvin Purvis wanted the agent who had counted and sealed it to open it so the chain of evidence could be accounted for. The correspondence leaves the petition’s result open. In the separate criminal proceeding, the Saint Paul jury acquitted Vidler in May 1935 and convicted Boss McLaughlin.

sourceLink.label: Read the Bureau’s account of the cashier and the two hats

title: The ransom note in the cornmeal box

blocks.text: A man in rough clothes left a package at the New Hotel Brunswick in Faribault. According to Arthur Murray’s witness outline, the man said his sick father needed medicine and would arrive on the 10:30 p.m. bus. Before the bus came, the man was back with a change of plan: his father had missed it. Would Murray hold the package?

No one came for the package. About a month later, Arthur’s mother opened it. A cornmeal box held a ransom note. It told the payoff man to get off in Owatonna, look for a black Chevrolet with a white dot on its spare tire cover, and find further instructions on the steering post.

By March 31, Bremer had already been released. George M. Murray told investigators that he forwarded the note that day to the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension in Saint Paul. The box itself made it onto a federal list of items to send to the U.S. attorney.

sourceLink.label: Open the Murray witness outlines in the FBI Vault

title: The Hudson that made its own smoke

blocks.text: In an Associated Press account, a black sedan drew up at the South Saint Paul post office with its siren blaring and smoke coming from the car. Two bank messengers carrying the Swift and Company payroll scrambled under a truck. Officer Leo Pavlak was killed and Officer John Yeaman was wounded. In 1935, the Associated Press reported that Dakota County Attorney Harold Stassen had linked the getaway car to a second robbery, in Chicago.

The federal report says a Hudson put up a smoke screen during a Chicago mail robbery in September 1933. After a collision, the men abandoned the car. It was a black 1933 Hudson. Investigators reported a siren, equipment for making a smoke screen, bullet-resistant glass at the driver’s door and steel plate around the sides. Investigators traced the modifications to a Chicago auto body shop.

Florida plates were mounted on the Hudson when it was abandoned. Inside, police found several other sets. One Minnesota pair had been issued for a Ford in Duluth. The federal report says Chicago police identified that pair as the plates seen on a car used in the South Saint Paul robbery. The number tied the car’s contents to the earlier payroll holdup.

sourceLink.label: Read the investigators’ description of the Hudson

title: The lamps at police headquarters

blocks.text: Wallace Jamie told the Saint Paul police he wanted to study their work. A 1936 magazine described his cover as an efficiency survey. Inside the public safety building, he was investigating ties between police and the underworld. A newspaper feature described microphones inside lamps and telephones. The magazine added hiding places under desks and chairs.

Every conversation Jamie took down in shorthand had to be transcribed. According to Modern Mechanix, a recorder called a pamograph cut conversations into an aluminum disc with a sapphire needle. Jamie also adapted a recorder used for fire alarm boxes. Its tape marked the digits dialed on a telephone line, so he could look for numbers that kept coming up.

A janitor working on a ventilation shaft found one of Jamie’s recorders, according to Modern Mechanix. The magazine said the recordings went to the mayor, the city attorney and the county attorney. Historian Anne E. Cowie describes a 1935 Ramsey County grand jury inquiry that followed Jamie’s work and returned twenty-one indictments.

sourceLink.label: Read the illustrated account of the microphones and ticker

title: The Phantom Gunman in Saint Paul

blocks.text: The Associated Press reported that California drug company cashier David Antink identified Morrie Moll in Saint Paul as a member of the crew that robbed him in 1923. The dispatch said police knew Moll as the Phantom Gunman. The alias Morrie Miller already appeared in the Gleeman brothers’ account of a Twin Cities liquor syndicate. Writer J. H. Graham places Antink’s identification in Governor Theodore Christianson’s office on June 5, 1929.

A United Press dispatch reported that Moll was released on $10,000 bail and quoted Los Angeles District Attorney Buron Fitts saying that Minnesota’s governor refused an extradition warrant. Graham writes that extradition was approved on June 15 and that Moll disappeared after his release on bond. The accounts agree that the transfer to California fell through.

After Antink was shot and killed in Hollywood in September, Fitts publicly blamed Saint Paul authorities and Los Angeles politicians for the failed transfer. The Associated Press reported that police sought Moll as a suspect. Four years later, a follow-up dispatch said the people who killed Antink had yet to be apprehended.

sourceLink.label: Read the September 27 dispatch

title: The bond in the food can

blocks.text: The Bureau’s history places Jess Doyle with the Barkers and Alvin Karpis at the Twin Oaks apartments in Saint Paul in 1932. By January 1935, when a federal grand jury in Saint Paul indicted Doyle in the Bremer kidnapping conspiracy case, he was living at 23 Warner Plaza in Kansas City. His companion told agents they went by Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Stacey there. The Saint Paul charges against Doyle were dismissed in May.

A telegram to FBI headquarters says agents searched Doyle’s apartment and skipped the food containers in the refrigerator. It also passes along a detail from the local press. A janitor reportedly found a stolen bond in a can left at the apartment and turned it over to police. The agent who sent the telegram said the office would check the report.

A later FBI letter confirms a $1,000 City of Peabody bond, serial number 56, was recovered at Doyle’s apartment. Volney Davis thought it came from an Oklahoma mail-truck robbery. The Bank of Drexel cashier identified it as one of the bonds taken from his bank in Missouri on December 13, 1934. The letter also says Doyle admitted robbing the bank with Davis and John Langdon. It records the match to the bank and leaves the exact circumstances of the find with the earlier press report.

sourceLink.label: Read the Kansas City telegram about the search

title: The alligator on the Lake Weir trail

blocks.text: On the way back to Chicago in early January 1935, Byron Bolton and William Harrison stopped at a pecan ranch south of Macon. In an outline of Bolton’s expected testimony, he recalled Russell Gibson and Doc Barker joining them and talking about deer, a motorboat, a cottage and a Florida lake with an alligator locals called Big Joe. In a longer interview, Bolton said he heard the men had tried to catch Big Joe with a small pig in a barrel. By their account, the alligator got the bait and escaped.

After a raid in Chicago, agents found two Florida maps in Doc Barker’s apartment. One marked Ocala and the other had a penciled ring around Lake Weir. The bureau’s February memorandum says agents showed the maps to Bolton on January 11. He thought the markings pointed to the hideout and told them about Highway 41 and Big Joe.

Agents checked the Ocala area from January 13 to 15 and located the Lake Weir cottage occupied by Fred and Kate Barker. The bureau’s 1936 summary, filed in the Saint Paul Bremer kidnapping investigation, calls the alligator Old Joe. It credits the marked map and the local alligator report as leads for the search.

title: Billie Frechette, in person

blocks.text: After the Lincoln Court shootout, Evelyn “Billie” Frechette was convicted in Saint Paul of conspiring to harbor a fugitive and sentenced to two years in prison. By July 1936, a trade paper was covering her next line of work. In a dispatch from a carnival in Johnstown, Pennsylvania, The Billboard listed her as an attraction in Scout Younger’s Arizona Dust Bowl.

The Billboard later reported that Frechette was appearing in theaters as the featured performer in Crime Does Not Pay. The trade paper described a group photograph. Alongside Frechette and the people who booked, advertised and introduced the act, it listed several wax figures.

Frank Heath saw posters in shop windows promising that Frechette would appear in person at the Haigler Theater. He thought she was back home in Wisconsin and suspected a promotional racket. On chamber of commerce stationery, he asked J. Edgar Hoover whether the woman could actually be Evelyn Frechette.

At a Pittsburgh carnival, Frechette talked about Dillinger and took questions. A stenographer from the local FBI office attended. He recognized her from photographs held by the Bureau, and the office sent Washington a report describing some of her answers.

title: The whiskey under the scrap iron

blocks.text: The federal indictment described freight cars from Winnipeg arriving in Minneapolis with barrels of whiskey under loads of scrap iron. It named two of the cars and gave three counts of barrels. In a later appeal, the federal court printed those entries. It also explained that importing the whiskey had already been illegal since 1917, even though these cars reached the rail sidings before national Prohibition went into effect.

At the removal hearing, Michael Weisman said he paid county attorney William Nash after hearing that the first car had been unloaded. He said he took the money from a bank vault. Justice Quinn’s later dissent set that story beside the railway records. The bank logged a visit on December 26. The railroad put the car in Saint Paul three days later and in Minneapolis on December 31.

A federal jury acquitted Nash. Governor J. A. A. Burnquist then heard a petition at the State Capitol in Saint Paul and removed him as Hennepin County attorney. The Minnesota Supreme Court left the removal in place. Its opinion explained that the governor was deciding whether Nash should remain in office. Justice Quinn dissented, questioning whether the record justified removal.

sourceLink.label: Read the opinions in the Nash removal case

title: The two Colts with aluminum grips

blocks.text: Two Minneapolis police officers were killed in the Third Northwestern National Bank robbery. On the getaway route through Como Park in Saint Paul, a Lincoln sedan was left disabled. J. H. Peterson testified that he drove past several men moving a white sack from the Lincoln to a smaller car. He identified Leonard Hankins, also known as Owen Lewis, as the man carrying it. Hankins was convicted of first-degree murder for his part in the robbery.

Police arrested Larry De Vol at a Saint Paul apartment and Hankins in Minneapolis. According to the court, each had a Colt with unusual aluminum grips in place of the standard checkered walnut. The factory numbers had been chiseled off both guns. A prosecution expert testified that the same tool made the marks on both. De Vol’s pistol also had an unusually long magazine.

Hankins said a man named Springer gave him the pistol the evening before his arrest. Witnesses for the state said they had seen him with a similar weapon earlier. A Saint Paul barber testified that he was cutting Hankins’s hair on Wabasha Street at a time that would have ruled out his participation. Hankins had told authorities before trial that he was on his way from Superior that afternoon and reached Saint Paul about five. The Minnesota Supreme Court affirmed the order denying him a new trial.

sourceLink.label: Read the Minnesota Supreme Court’s comparison of the pistols

title: The telephone pole that stopped Touhy

blocks.text: A car carrying Roger Touhy, Eddie McFadden, Gus Schaefer and Willie Sharkey skidded into a telephone pole near Elkhorn, Wisconsin. The Kewaskum Statesman identified Harry Ward as the unarmed officer who stopped the men. The Illinois Supreme Court later dated the wreck to July 19, 1933 and described guns seized from the car.

In his 1959 memoir, Touhy said he agreed to pay $22.50 for the pole. Walworth County’s history says Ward brought the men in to settle the damage. It adds that Sharkey hitched a ride on a chicken truck to Lake Geneva and called the jail about the pole. A deputy arrested him there.

On July 22, the Manchester Evening Herald printed a picture of Elkhorn deputies holding Touhy and billed it as his first newspaper or police photograph. By August, federal officers had taken the four men to Saint Paul to face charges in William Hamm Jr.’s kidnapping. A jury acquitted all four on the federal Hamm counts in November.

sourceLink.label: See the July 22 front page

title: The wedding and the two calls

blocks.text: A Bureau memorandum says Bruno Austin, also known as Bruno Putis, was taken into custody at the conclusion of his Chicago wedding ceremony. Two days later a Saint Paul grand jury returned an indictment in the Bremer kidnapping conspiracy. It listed a man called Whitey. The Bureau later identified Whitey as Austin.

Two calls came while Mrs. Austin was out, according to her account to Special Agent M. Shafetz. Her mother answered both. The callers claimed to be federal men and said they wanted to question Mrs. Austin. A week later, she went to the Chicago Bureau office to ask whether the calls were theirs. Shafetz told her neither had come from the Bureau.

The Bureau named Austin among the defendants when the Bremer trial opened in Saint Paul in April. On May 6, the court ordered him discharged from custody. The Bureau’s summary then records a rearrest in Chicago and an October murder conviction there in a separate case.

sourceLink.label: Read Shafetz’s report on the two calls

title: The manhunt at the clothing counter

blocks.text: Police in Atlantic City traced a Buick to a garage and went to the hotel where Alvin Karpis and Harry Campbell were staying. The Bureau’s later summary describes a man in the hallway in his underwear offering to fetch the person the officers wanted. Karpis got into Campbell’s room. The two men fired on the officers and escaped. Dolores Delaney was wounded in the exchange. Two days later, a Saint Paul indictment named both men in the Edward Bremer kidnapping case.

Police asked for a warning to go out to clothing stores. An Associated Press dispatch said Karpis escaped in slippers, trousers and an overcoat. It listed slippers and an overcoat for Campbell too, with underwear instead of trousers. Authorities told the press they were certain the two were still on the island. The three highway bridges were under guard.

The Bureau’s later summary puts the men in a stolen Pontiac that they abandoned near Quakertown, Pennsylvania. It says they left Atlantic City in the car and took another one near Sellersville after abducting its driver. The shop warning reflected the police’s early belief. The later summary traces the escape beyond the island and gives no clothing-store stop.

sourceLink.label: Read the clothing-store warning

title: The mailbags they locked again

blocks.text: Federal prosecutor Thomas J. Morrissey told the United Press that Jack Segar of Saint Paul went to Denver in 1931 and obtained railroad switch keys and keys that fit post office mailbags. Morrissey said Segar returned to Saint Paul and recruited a crew there, including John Edwards and a man known as Walker.

Morrissey said the crew chose small-town stations where mail sat overnight or waited for a train. They allegedly opened the mailroom with the switch keys, used the other keys on the sacks, took the registered mail and then locked the sacks and the building again.

Morrissey told the United Press that a $100 Liberty bond passed by a Denver relief worker had led investigators to more than two dozen mail thefts. The May 9 report said eleven people were under arrest, with Segar and Winston W. Clement, identified as Walker, held in Saint Paul. The dispatch ends with the arrests.
